name: Gareth Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, and nothing gets linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a backend developer at a payroll software company, about ninety people, and my team looks after the engine that works out tax and pension deductions for around four hundred client firms. Most mornings start with a stand-up, then I'm in old Java code that's older than some of my colleagues' careers. I like it because it's precise; if a number is off by one cent, somebody's wage slip is wrong, and I'm the one who finds why. What wears me out is the end of the tax year, when every rule change lands at once and we work late for three weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you look after old code. Do you use any of the AI coding tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. The company switched on a code assistant in everyone's editor last spring, and I turned mine off the same afternoon. I don't trust code I didn't reason through myself, especially when it touches people's pay. Priya, who sits next to me, uses it all day, and we argue about it over lunch in a friendly way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, though maybe more politely at work. I'd tell people the hype was mostly investors talking up their own shares, and that the boring work of getting payroll right still needs people who care. Online I'd probably share a long post about how much money and electricity was burned on chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my life carries on. My job is safe, the pay is good, and my partner and I keep saving for a flat. The only thing that changes is that I'd stop feeling like the odd one out for switching the assistant off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep working on the payroll engine, keep putting a fixed amount into savings every month, and maybe finally push for the union branch some of us talked about last year. I'd say yes to running the tax-year release again, because that's where I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, which isn't my best quality. It feels like the world I trained for is still the world I live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a union branch. Why would that matter if nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the pressure doesn't need AI to exist. Management already counts tickets closed per week and compares us, and that gets worse every year whether the chatbot works or not. A union would give us a say in how we're measured, and in this version of things I'd have the energy to help set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your day the routine automation would still take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the release notes and the test data we write by hand. I wouldn't miss writing test payslips for imaginary people called Test Testerson. If that goes, fine, as long as nobody pretends it means they need fewer of us.

say: I'd say the AI boom was mostly **investor hype**, and careful payroll work still needs people.
I'd post about how much **money and power** went into chatbots for very little.
think: My **job is safe**, the pay stays good and our flat savings keep growing.
I'd stop feeling like the **odd one out** for switching the assistant off.
do: Keep working on the **payroll engine** and lead the tax-year release again.
Keep a **fixed monthly amount** going into the flat savings.
Help start the **union branch** that colleagues discussed last year.
feel: **Relieved** that the work he trained for still matters, and a little smug about it.
S0.quote: I wouldn't miss writing test payslips for imaginary people called Test Testerson.
fieldNote: He switched off the company **code assistant** on day one and still sees that as a matter of care, not fear.
Even in the calm picture he wants a **union** because management already measures tickets per week.
His security comes from **strong savings**, good pay and plenty of similar jobs nearby.

steps.text: Keep maintaining the payroll engine and lead the tax-year release
Put a fixed sum into the flat deposit savings every month
Help set up a union branch at the payroll company

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on how AI gets used before anyone touches headcount. With friends I'd be blunter: this is a transfer from people who write code to people who own the company. Online I'd share the union's line and probably get into arguments with people who think it's all progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm in trouble faster than most. Coding is right there on the list, and I'm the one person on my team who refuses the tools. If management decides four people with AI can do what seven did, I'm an obvious name to drop, average skill and stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd join the tech workers' union properly and push for a written agreement on AI and job cuts. I'd move more of my pay into savings, so I'd have a year covered instead of nine months. And I'd grudgingly sit the company's AI training, because refusing it outright would just hand them the excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. I like to think I'm principled, but picturing this I feel more cornered than principled. My partner would tell me I'm catastrophising, and she's often right, but not always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sit the training but you said you don't trust the tools. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent wins, I suppose. I'd learn enough to show I can use the assistant, and I'd still check every line it writes on the payroll engine by hand. Maybe that turns out to be the skill they need: the person who doesn't believe the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, oddly, even though she loves the tools. She's the fastest at the routine tickets, and the routine tickets are exactly what the software takes first. Martin, our team lead, would be fine; he spends his day in meetings that nobody can automate because nobody understands them.

say: I'd say we need **written rules** on AI use before any job cuts.
I'd tell friends this moves money from **coders to owners**, and argue it online.
think: Coding is first in line, and as the **only refuser** on my team I'm an easy cut.
My **average skill** plus stubbornness makes me a visible name on any list.
do: Join the **tech workers' union** and push for a written AI agreement.
Raise savings from nine months to **a full year** of costs.
Sit the **company AI training** so refusing it can't be used against me.
feel: **Cornered** more than principled, with a tight feeling in his chest.
S1.quote: Maybe that turns out to be the skill they need: the person who doesn't believe the machine.
fieldNote: He knows his **refusal** of AI tools makes him visible, and that sharpens his fear.
He would **bend on training** because of rent, while still checking every line by hand.
He worries about a colleague who uses AI most, seeing **routine tickets** as first to go.

steps.text: Join the tech workers' union and push for an AI agreement
Grow savings from nine months to a full year of costs
Complete the company's AI assistant training course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to step in, and fast: tax the firms that replace staff and pay people while they find their feet. At work I'd be in every union meeting. Online I'd probably be angry in a way I'd regret later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year or two of 2028. Payroll code is pure thinking work at a desk; there's no hands-on part to hide in. The three-year gap before robots doesn't help me at all, because I don't touch anything physical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, with two years' warning, I'd stop spending on anything big and get to eighteen months of savings. I'd look into a trade where the robots come later, maybe electrical work, because three extra years is something. Once it arrives, I'd sign up for whatever public support exists and use the union to fight for a long notice period and decent payouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really scared. I'm twenty-seven and I thought I had forty years of this. My partner's a nurse, and the strange thing is she'd suddenly be the safe one in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a trade. Can you see yourself doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not happily. I've never wired a plug in my life, and I'd be an apprentice next to teenagers. But I'd rather be a slow apprentice in 2029 than a fast developer with no job in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat. We'd stop looking at flats immediately, because a mortgage on a job that disappears in two years is madness. Then the holidays, then the car, which we barely use anyway.

say: I'd demand that governments **tax firms** that replace staff and fund people between jobs.
I'd be in every **union meeting** and probably too angry online.
think: My payroll job is pure **desk work**, so I expect it gone soon after 2028.
The **three-year robot gap** doesn't help someone who never touches anything physical.
do: Build savings to **eighteen months** and stop all big spending now.
Look into an **electrical apprenticeship**, where robots arrive about three years later.
Use the union to push for **long notice** and fair payouts.
feel: **Scared**, because he expected forty working years and now sees two.
Oddly aware that his nurse partner becomes the **safe earner** at home.
S2.quote: I'd rather be a slow apprentice in 2029 than a fast developer with no job in 2028.
fieldNote: He sees no **hands-on shelter** in his own work, so the robot delay is irrelevant to him.
The **flat purchase** is the first thing he would drop.
A resistant person reaching for a **trade he's never tried** shows how cornered he feels.

steps.text: Build savings to eighteen months and freeze big purchases
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship starting in 2028
Push through the union for long notice and fair payouts
Stop looking at flats with his partner until work is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get a law on the books about retraining money and notice periods, so let's not waste them. I'd try to be the calm voice in the union chat instead of the angry one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years just moves my end date. I'd be thirty-two when AGI lands, which is still early enough to start over, but I'd have spent the time knowing. I'm not sure the extra time helps someone like me who doesn't move until he's pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep the payroll job, because it's still paying well, and save hard toward two years of costs. I'd start evening classes in electrical installation, slowly, one module at a time. And I'd stay active in the union so there's something in place by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like a slow leak. Less panic than the two-year one, more dread. I'd probably be short with my partner more often and not know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't move until you're pushed. Would you actually start those classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I might sign up and then skip half of them. That's the pattern with me. If my partner signed me up and drove me there, it'd happen; if it's left to me, I'd find reasons the time isn't right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents I'm fine and that I'm saving. My dad worked in a printing plant that closed, and he never said a word about it until it was over. I'd probably do the same thing, which is not something I'm proud of.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to pass laws on retraining money and notice.
I'd try to be the **calm voice** in the union chat.
think: Five years only **moves my end date**; I'd be thirty-two when it lands.
Extra time may not help someone who **only moves when pushed**.
do: Keep the payroll job and save toward **two years** of costs.
Start **evening classes** in electrical installation, one module at a time.
Stay active in the **union** so protections exist by 2031.
feel: A slow **dread** rather than panic, leaking into home life.
S3.quote: My dad worked in a printing plant that closed, and he never said a word about it until it was over.
fieldNote: He admits he might **skip the classes** he plans to take.
His father's **printing plant closure** shapes how he would hide worry from family.
More time lowers his panic but not his expectation of **losing the job**.

steps.text: Save toward two years of living costs while still employed
Enrol in evening classes in electrical installation
Stay active in the union to win protections before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if we let companies use it alone. I'd push for public retraining schemes that start now, not in 2035. Online I'd share the policy stuff, not the doom stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably keep doing what I'm doing for too long. I'd be thirty-seven, still young, but I'd have fewer years left of good developer pay than I thought. It feels survivable, but I don't trust myself to use the time well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep saving and keep the job. I'd look at a slow move toward work with a hands-on part, maybe installing and maintaining payroll terminals and clocking systems on site. And I'd vote and campaign for the retraining money, because that's what would actually help people like Priya.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not frightened. It's more like knowing you'll have to move house in ten years: annoying, sad, but there's time. I'd still feel a bit of a coward for not adapting sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you use the ten years well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline I can't argue with, honestly. If the union or the government set out a clear plan, like retraining money that opens in 2030, I'd follow it. Left to myself I'd keep fixing the payroll engine until the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and your partner change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still buy the flat, but a smaller one, so one wage could cover it. My partner and I talked about kids someday; I'd want her nursing pay to be enough on its own before we do that.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** only if companies don't control it alone.
I'd push for **public retraining** schemes that start now.
think: With a decade, I'd probably **keep going too long** in the same job.
I'd be **thirty-seven** at arrival, with fewer good-pay years than planned.
do: Keep the job and keep **saving** every month.
Move gradually toward **on-site work** like installing clocking systems.
Vote and campaign for **retraining money** that opens years before 2036.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than frightened, plus a little shame at adapting slowly.
S4.quote: Left to myself I'd keep fixing the payroll engine until the last day.
fieldNote: He trusts **outside deadlines** more than his own will to change.
He would buy a **smaller flat** sized to one wage.
Even with a decade, he still expects his **coding income** to end, so the worry stays real.

steps.text: Keep saving monthly while staying in the payroll job
Move toward on-site installation of clocking and payroll terminals
Campaign for public retraining money that opens before 2036
Buy a smaller flat that his partner's wage alone could cover

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt. There's no hands-on part of my job to buy me time, and I'm slow to change. What would help is money that pays people while they retrain, a proper notice period by law, and honestly someone who tells me exactly which course to take.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who people blame. I'd blame the owners and investors, not the engineers who build the tools; Priya builds things with them and she's no villain. I'd want people to remember that when it happens.

headlineQuote: There's no hands-on part of my job to buy me time, and I'm slow to change.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** backend developer on a payroll engine, living with his nurse partner and saving for a flat.
He switched off the **code assistant** on day one and checks every line affecting people's pay.
He is **progressive**, wants a union and blames owners and investors rather than engineers.
His worry climbs steeply as AGI gets closer, because his work has **no hands-on part**.
He knows he only **moves when pushed** and wants clear outside deadlines and support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his desk job has nothing hands-on and he is slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, a legal notice period and someone telling him exactly which course to take.
